job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I'm at the kitchen table in our flat in Manchester by half past eight, with my laptop and a cold tea. I live with my parents and my little sister, so I try to be out of the way before my dad gets back from the night shift driving his taxi. I send out a few applications, do a couple of hours of online maths tutoring for school kids, and spend the afternoon on a small electronics project so I don't feel I'm just sitting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what did you do for your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical engineering. My final project was a solar charge controller for a bike light, and it worked on the bench but I never got it running reliably outside. I passed, nothing flashy. I had no internship because the ones I applied for wanted second-year students with a placement already, which was a loop I couldn't break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've heard this before and the sky didn't fall. At home my dad would say it's the same with every new gadget, and I'd agree. Online I'd stay quiet, though I might share an article saying people should wait for evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's the best of the options for me, because the jobs still exist, they're just hard to get. I use an AI tool now and then for drafting emails, and if it saves routine time then entry-level tasks might get a bit thinner. But my real problem is that nobody's hiring juniors in this city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aiming at around thirty a month, and I'd spend more time on the tutoring since that's the only income I have. I'd also ask my old lecturer whether any local firms need a junior for testing. I'd put my project on a small portfolio page, which I haven't done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. Not great, not terrible. I'm anxious about the debt and about my parents, who are tired, but I don't feel the ground is shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real problem is nobody hiring juniors. What have you noticed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most listings say two to three years' experience for an entry-level role, which makes no sense. I counted fourteen suitable entry-level jobs within an hour's commute in October, and about two hundred people apply to each. So a pass degree with no internship barely gets read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your parents feel about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum cleans offices in the mornings, and she asks every night if there's news. My dad never says anything, but he stopped telling me how much he made that week. I think he doesn't want me to feel I owe them, which makes it worse.

say: I'd say we've heard this before and **the sky didn't fall**.
Online I'd stay quiet but maybe share an article about waiting for evidence.
think: The jobs still exist; the real problem is **no junior hiring** in Manchester.
My occasional AI use might thin out routine entry-level tasks slightly.
do: Send about **thirty applications** a month and ask my old lecturer about local testing roles.
Put my solar controller project on a small **portfolio page**.
Do more maths tutoring, my only income.
feel: Okay, honestly: **anxious** about debt, but not about the ground shifting.
Worried about tired parents and my father's silence about money.
S0.quote: I counted fourteen suitable entry-level jobs within an hour's commute in October, and about two hundred people apply to each.
fieldNote: Steady and measured; his worry is the local job count rather than AI.
Dad's silence about **money** shows the family pressure he carries.
Uses AI sparingly and sees it as minor.

steps.text: Send thirty job applications a month
Take on more online maths tutoring students
Build a portfolio page showing the solar charge controller

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and we should plan for it rather than argue about it. To my friends from uni I'd say learn the tools now, because the tasks that went first at my cousin's company were the checking and coding. Online I'd back stronger rules so firms can't cut staff and call it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, entry-level engineering is the soft target. The junior work, testing code, drawing up simple circuits, writing specs, is what software can do. It means I might not get a first job in electrical at all, and may need to come in sideways through support or technician work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools every day instead of now and then, to prove I can work with them, not just around them. I'd take a short course in embedded systems or cloud basics, something with a certificate. And I'd apply for technician jobs at the energy firms near the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not frozen. I've got more energy than I had in the slow one, because now there's something to do. But my debt is still there and I know I'm already behind people with placements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does using the tools every day look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write my cover letters with help, then rewrite them in my own voice. I'd use it to explain circuits I find confusing, and to generate test cases for code. I'd keep a log of what the AI tool got wrong, so I can show an employer I check its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your cousin's company. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ravi works in a software firm, and they stopped hiring graduates for testing last spring. They said the tooling does most of it now. He kept his job because he moved into customer-facing work, which is why I think the sideways route is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough and that governments must act now. I'd tell my friends we need a basic income or paid retraining on the table before 2028, not after. Online I'd share the sensible plans and ignore the doomsayers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels like I've trained for a job that vanishes before I get it. Thinking work is exactly what AGI does, and the jobs I want are thinking jobs with a bit of hardware. I'd have less than two years to find a way in, and I'd be competing with software that never sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for anything with hands in it: field technician, installation, maintenance at the energy firms. I'd learn some practical wiring, since robots take till 2031. I'd also push my dad to sign up for any local advice sessions and I'd go to my MP's surgery, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Because I'd be doing all this on tutoring money. My parents have no spare cash, and if my dad's taxi work dried up because of self-driving cars, we'd be in real trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your MP at the surgery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what is being done for people who graduate into this. Specifically, whether loan repayments pause and whether there's funded retraining. I'd bring my savings figure, which is about three hundred pounds, so it's real and not abstract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned self-driving cars. How does that connect for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad has driven a taxi for twenty years. If thinking AI arrives in 2028 and then robots and driving automation follow, his job is at risk by 2031. So both of us could lose income close together, which is the thing I can't stop thinking about.

say: I'd tell friends we need **paid retraining** or basic income agreed before 2028.
Online I'd share sensible plans and ignore the doomsayers.
think: I've trained for a job that **vanishes** before I get it.
My dad's taxi work could also be hit within a few years.
do: Apply for **hands-on jobs**: field technician, installation and maintenance.
Learn practical wiring, since robot hands arrive later around 2031.
Go to my **MP's surgery** with my savings figure of three hundred pounds.
feel: Scared, because all this rests on **tutoring money**.
Terrified that my dad's income and mine could go in the same years.
S2.quote: My dad has driven a taxi for twenty years. If thinking AI arrives in 2028 and then robots and driving automation follow, his job is at risk by 2031.
fieldNote: The **household** earner is at risk too, which raises his mood to alarmed.
Turns toward hands-on work because he understands the robot delay.
Goes to political action only when it seems **necessary**.

steps.text: Apply for field technician and installation jobs
Learn practical wiring at an evening course
Go to the MP's surgery and ask about funded retraining
Ask the council about advice sessions for my father

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance. I'd tell friends to use the time well and to push for rules about who benefits. Online I'd argue that firms profiting from AI should help pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I could still build an actual career if I get a first job in the next twelve months. I'd have time to get a few years of experience before AGI hits in 2031. It's a hard window, but a real one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first technician or support job offered and learn on the job. I'd keep using AI tools and add a cloud or embedded certificate in the first year. I'd also save a tenth of any wages and try to help my parents build a small buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but there's something to hold on to. It's not the sinking feeling I had with 2028. I'd feel more like a man running for a train that hasn't left yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the two-year world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me take a boring first job without feeling it's a waste. In two years I'd be panicking and snatching at anything. With five I can pick something that builds skills, even slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Dina is fifteen and wants to study engineering. I'd tell her to still study it but to learn how to work with AI, and to pick a branch with some hands-on in it. I'd say don't copy me exactly, but don't give up either.

I'd argue firms profiting from AI should help pay for retraining.
think: I could still build a **career** if I get a first job within a year.
Experience gained before 2031 gives me a real, if hard, window.

Add a cloud or embedded certificate in the first year.
Save a tenth of wages and help my parents build a **small buffer**.

steps.text: Take the first technician or support job offered
Add a cloud or embedded certificate in year one
Save a tenth of every wage into a buffer for my parents
Advise my sister Dina to study engineering with a hands-on branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and a waste if they don't. I'd tell friends to pick skills that will still matter, like systems thinking and hands-on testing. I'd back political action to protect people through the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years means I could build a whole first career before AGI arrives. I'd be thirty-three in 2036. I could work in energy or hardware for several years, pay off my debt, and maybe move up into something robots can't do fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any entry job in the first year and aim to leave it within three for a better one. I'd study part-time for a master's in power systems if an employer would help pay. I'd start saving a little, and put some into a pension, which I haven't thought about before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, in a careful way. Not because it's safe, but because I can see a path with steps in it. I'd still worry in the years when AGI is a few years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which years would worry you most along the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably 2033 to 2035, as thinking AI is already there and the robots are close. By then I'd be thirty and need to know my place. If I haven't built something by then, I might not have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do, if you had one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a proper training plan, not just a laptop and good luck. And honesty, if my role was likely to go, so I could plan. I'd trade a bit of pay for a clear plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Nobody would have time to plan, and my dad's job and mine could both go close together. What would help is a clear public plan: paid retraining, a pause on loan repayments, and firms taking on graduates in return for the benefits AI brings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume graduates are comfortable. I'm in a flat with four people, three hundred pounds in the bank and a degree that nobody seems to want. I'm not complaining, I'd just like someone to hear how ordinary and tight this is.

headlineQuote: I'm in a flat with four people, three hundred pounds in the bank and a degree that nobody seems to want.
portrait: **Wei**, 23, graduated in electrical engineering with a pass and no internship, and lives with his parents and sister in Manchester.
His father drives a taxi and his mother cleans offices, so there is **no family money** to lean on.
He earns a little tutoring maths online and uses AI tools **now and then**.
Leaning left, he wants public support and rules, but he also acts: certificates, technician jobs and a visit to his MP.
His mood moves from anxious to alarmed when his father's taxi work and his own jobs seem to be at risk together.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries him most because there'd be no time to plan.
He fears his father's taxi income and his own jobs could go together.
whatWouldHelp: A clear public plan with **paid retraining** and a pause on loan repayments.
Firms that take on graduates in return for the benefits AI gives them.
